opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, honestly, I think the model picker is one of those things we should feel a little embarrassed about. If you step back and look at it from a user's perspective, you open the app and you're asked to make a decision you're not really equipped to make. Do I want the big one, the fast one, the one with extended thinking? Most people don't know, and they shouldn't have to know. That's our job.

So the direction I'd love to see us go, and the one I think makes the most sense, is that for the vast majority of people the default should just work. You ask a question, and the system figures out how much effort that question deserves. If you're asking what to make for dinner, you don't need the model to sit there and think for two minutes. If you're debugging a gnarly distributed systems issue, you probably want it to slow down and really reason. The model itself is increasingly good at telling the difference, so we should lean on that rather than pushing the decision onto the user.

At the same time, I don't think you remove control entirely. Power users and developers really care about this. They have cost constraints, latency budgets, they've tuned their prompts against a particular model. So for them, explicit choice is a feature, not a bug. The trick is layering it: sensible automatic defaults on top, and the knobs are there if you go looking for them.

The other piece is communication. When we do expose choices, they should be described in terms of what you're trying to do, not in terms of our internal naming. "Quick answers" versus "deep work" is a lot more meaningful to someone than a version number. And I think being transparent about what the system chose, so if it decided to think harder, it tells you, builds trust and helps people learn when to override it.

Ultimately, the goal is that people stop thinking about models at all and just think about getting their work done. Every moment someone spends staring at a dropdown is a moment we've failed a little bit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model choices and automatic effort, but does not present a cost–performance Pareto frontier as the organizing principle for Anthropic’s lineup.

r002.rationale: It recommends automatic selection of how much effort a question gets, but does not clearly describe a routing layer choosing among models based on the request’s cost–intelligence tradeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, honestly I think the current state of model selection is kind of a failure on our part, and on the industry's part generally. If you're a developer or a regular person and you open up a product and you see a dropdown with five names and version numbers, that's us pushing complexity onto you that you shouldn't have to deal with. Most people don't want to think about whether they need the big model or the fast model. They just want the thing to work and to be good.

So the direction I'd like to see us go is a few things. One, the default should just be right most of the time. The product should pick. If you're asking a quick factual question, you don't need the most expensive, slowest model thinking hard for thirty seconds. If you're asking it to refactor a large codebase or reason through something genuinely hard, you do. The system should be able to route that, or at least adapt how much effort it spends, without you flipping a switch.

Two, when you do expose choice, it should be framed in terms people actually care about, not in terms of our internal naming. Nobody wakes up thinking "I need Opus today." They think "I need this to be really careful" or "I need this to be cheap and fast because I'm running it a million times." The tradeoff is basically quality versus cost and latency, and we should just say that plainly.

And three, I think the naming itself needs to get simpler and more stable over time. Every time we ship a new generation we're asking people to relearn the landscape, and that's a tax. The ideal is that you have a very small number of options, the names mean something intuitive, and the newer one is just straightforwardly better so you don't have to think about it.

The deeper thing is that as these models get more capable, the model itself should be doing more of this work. It should know when it's out of its depth, know when to think longer, know when a cheaper path is fine. The user choosing a model is kind of a transitional artifact. I'd like to see it mostly disappear.

r002.rationale: It recommends that the product route requests to an appropriate model or adjust effort automatically, using examples that distinguish quick, inexpensive tasks from difficult tasks warranting more reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think we should take more of that decision off the user’s plate. Most people don’t want to study a model lineup and figure out which one has the right tradeoff between speed, cost, and capability. They want to ask a question and get a useful answer.

So ideally, you tell us what you’re trying to accomplish, and the system chooses an appropriate model. For a simple question, you want a fast response. For a difficult problem, you might want it to spend more time thinking. We should make that feel natural, while still giving people explicit control when they want it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should do more of that work for the user. Most people don’t want to study a model lineup and figure out the tradeoffs between intelligence, speed, and cost. They want to get something done.

Ideally, you tell Claude what you’re trying to do, and we pick the right model behind the scenes. If it’s a simple question, you should get a fast answer. If it’s a really hard problem, we should spend more time thinking about it. And then, for developers and people who want that control, you can still expose the individual models. But understanding our product lineup shouldn’t be a prerequisite for using the product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model tradeoffs but does not present a cost–performance Pareto frontier as the lineup’s organizing principle.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing a model behind the scenes based on task difficulty, but does not clearly say the routing decision should use the cost–intelligence tradeoff the request warrants.
